# Assessment of owl limpet (*Lottia gigantea*) populations at sites within Crystal Cove State Marine Conservation Area

```{r load packages, include = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
```

## Project Summary:

*Once you have completed this entire assignment, come back and write a project summary here that covers the aims, research questions, and basic methods of this study.*

My summary response:

For this project, our class looked at owl limpet populations at Crystal Cove's marine protected area (MPA) to see how their size, crowding and behavior changes depending on where they live. We used field data that has been collected from 2022-2025 across four sites: Corona del Mar, Treasure Cove, Heisler Park and Shaws Cove. Though on our actual field trip data we weren't able to collect any data (due to the high tide), we conducted a simulated data collection day the following week back on campus. Through this project, we were interested in learning if human foot traffic or different habitats (open rock or mussel patches) affected how big the limpets grew. Different groups used different survey lengths, so we turned our raw counts into a standardized "limpets per square meter" metric. We did this so that we could compare crowding across all four sites in a fair manner. We also investigated how the owl limpets protect their home by running log models to discover how a limpet's body weight matches against the size of the territory it calls home/defends. Additionally, we ran statistical tests, including t-tests and ANOVAs on our data. This assignment allowed us to clearly observe how the local environment stress impact how the limpets navigate their life and survive.

You have been given data from several locations and survey years:

- 2022: Corona del Mar (CDM) - size data only, taken haphazardly

- 2023: Treasure Cove (TC) - size data in 5-m transects, territories

- 2024: Heisler Park and Shaws Cove - size data in variable length transects, territories

- 2025: Treasure Cove (TC) - size data in 5-m transects, territories

```{r}

SizeData_2022_2025
```

THINKING QUESTIONS: Do we have the number of transects that we expect to in our data set? Are they all the same length? Do our numbers make sense?

ANSWER: Our methods have been a little inconsistent. We used different methods at Shaws Cove and Heisler than we did at Treasure Cove. At Treasure Cove, we have used 5 meter long set length transects. At Shaws Cove and Heisler, we ran transects of variable length from the high tide line to the lowest accessible part of the intertidal. In order to compare population density, we will need to eventually divide by transect length/area to get limpets per square meter.

```{r}
No_CDM_Sizes
```

#### 2.1. How many limpets did we measure at each site in each year for sizes?

Use nrow(), group_by() and count() to tally the limpet observations at each transect. We used the same transect numbers at Shaws and Heisler, so group_by() site as well.

```{r}

  nrow()
```

#### 2.2 What was the limpet density (i.e., limpets per square meter) for each transect?

Make a new dataframe out of the `No_CDM_Sizes` that has a column called *density,* that calculates the limpets per square meter for each transect. Remember that the transect included 1 meter on either side of the tape (total of 2 meters wide). Make sure to maintain the separation in year for the two Treasure Cove surveys using the `group_by()` function.

```{r}
# creating a new dataframe from filtered data
Limpet_Density <- No_CDM_Sizes |>
# keeping only these four columns, but dropping all others
  select(transect_length_m, site, transect_num, year) |> 
# group the dataset by all four columns
  group_by(transect_length_m, site, transect_num, year) |> 
# count the number of owl limpets in each transect
  summarise(count = n()) |> 
# creating a new 'density' column by dividing count by the area
  mutate(density = count/(transect_length_m*2))
# print completed density data 
Limpet_Density
```

Do you see any patterns just from examining this table of values?

When examining the table of values, there are a few things that immediately stand out. First, if looking at the transect_length_m column, we can see that the fieldwork was done differently across each site. At Treasure Cove, the length of the transects is always exactly 5 meters, where at the other sites, the transects change on ever row. We can also see that the count column displays that some transects have lots of limpets accounted for and others have very little.

#### 2.2. Calculating mean and standard error of population density

What was the mean limpets per square meter across all sites? And the standard deviation? And standard error?

```{r}
Limpet_Density$density |> 
#calculating mean
  mean()

Limpet_Density$density |> 
# calculating standard deviation
  sd()

n <- Limpet_Density$density |> 
# counting the amount of transects
  length()

Limpet_Density$density |> 
# calculating the standard error
  sd()/sqrt(n)
```

Now create a summary table in which you calculate separate mean and standard deviation for each site and year (Shaws vs. Heisler vs. Treasure Cove)? What was the standard error? Round the mean and standard error to one decimal place. (look up the `round()` function!)

```{r}
# use summarize() to calculate the mean and standard error (sd/sqrt(n)) for the two locations
## creating a new dataframe
LimpetPopSummary <- Limpet_Density |>
## grouping by site and year
  group_by(site, year)|> 
## condensing rows into summary stats, skipping missing data
  summarise(mean_density = mean(density, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_density = sd(density, na.rm = TRUE), 
            n = n(), # count
            se_density = sd_density/sqrt(n)) |>  # standard error
## rounding function, limit to 2 decimal places
  mutate_at(vars(mean_density, sd_density, se_density), # bonus line to reduce digits
            .funs = round, 2) 
# Display your summary nicely using kable(). 
knitr::kable(LimpetPopSummary)
```

Based on these plots, does your data meet assumptions for a t-test?

T-Test assumptions (for a Student's T-test)

- Are the data continuous (i.e., not categorical/discrete)?

- Have the sample data been randomly sampled from a population?

- Is there homogeneity of variance (i.e., the variability of the data in each group is similar)?

- Is the distribution of the model residuals approximately normal?

Is it roughly the same so that we can compare? Is it enough to run a statistical test?

```{r}
Limpet_Density |> 
# grouping by site and year
  group_by(site, year) |> 
# condensing rows to non-repeating transect numbers from each group
  summarise(sample_size = n_distinct(transect_num),

            .groups = "drop")
```

#### 2.6. Does average number of owl limpets per square meter differ significantly between Heisler Park and Shaws Cove?

Filter the data to only include those sites before putting it into the `t.test()` function. These are a good comparison because they were measured in the same year with the same survey methods.

```{r t-test}
# run a t-test on your count data from each site (Limpet_Density)
ShawsHeislerDensity <- Limpet_Density |> 
# keeping rows where the site is exactly 'Heisler Park' or 'Shaws Cove'
  filter(site == "Heisler Park" | site == "Shaws Cove")
# performing independent two-sample t-test
t.test(density ~ site, data = ShawsHeislerDensity)
```

#### 2.8 EXTRA CREDIT: Do an ANOVA comparing Shaws, Heisler, and Treasure Cove 2025 density data (exclude 2023 so that the sample size is similar between all three). Use a Tukey post-hoc test. Explain the results.

```{r}
anova_density_data <- Limpet_Density |> 
  filter(year == "2025" | year == "2024")
# fitting linear regression model predicting density based on site
Limpet_Density_model <- lm(density ~ site, data = anova_density_data)
# creating boxplot to compare density distribution across all sites
ggplot(anova_density_data) +
  aes(x = site, y = density) +
  geom_boxplot()
# creating QQ plot to check if model residuals are normally distributed
plot(Limpet_Density_model, which = 2)
# running Shapiro-Wilk test to test assumptions of normality
shapiro.test(Limpet_Density_model$residuals)
# runnning Barlett test to investigate the assumption of variance across sites
bartlett.test(density ~ site, data = anova_density_data)
# print ANOVA summary table
anova(Limpet_Density_model)
# performing Tukey HSD post-hoc test
TukeyHSD(aov(density ~ site, data = anova_density_data))
```

#### 3.2. Is there a [statistically significant]{.underline} difference in [mean]{.underline} size between limpets measured at Treasure Cove (a relatively low-impact site) compared to CDM (a high impact site)?

We have a much larger sample size for shell lengths than we did for density, so we can apply our tests of assumptions more rigorously and demonstrate our various tests.

##### 3.2.1 [Determine whether a parametric or non-parametric test is appropriate.]{.underline}

T-Test assumptions (for a Student's T-test)

- Are the data continuous (i.e., not categorical/discrete)? **YES**

- Have the sample data been randomly sampled from a population? **(Yes)**

- Is there homogeneity of variance (i.e., the variability of the data in each group is similar)? **NO**

```{r}
## Test for Homogeneity of Variance with an F-Test

# create the appropriate filter to include only Treasure Cove and CDM data
CDM_TC_Sizes <- SizeData_2022_2025 |> 
  filter(site == "Treasure Cove" | site == "Corona del Mar")
  
# set the linear model for testing the assumptions
model <- lm(shell_length_mm ~ site, data = CDM_TC_Sizes)

# Examine plot of Residuals vs. Fitted values
plot(model, which = 1)

# F-test for homogeneity of variance - if p-value < 0.05 then variances are different. 
var.test(shell_length_mm ~ site, data = CDM_TC_Sizes)

# NOTE: if your sample fails this test, have no fear! Welch's t-test (the default that R uses) is okay to use with unequal variances. 

```

- Is the distribution of the model residuals approximately normal?

  No because the distribution of residuals has data clumping on both ends, rather than an even distribution around the fitted line.

```{r}
## Test for normality

# examine a QQ-plot
plot(model, which = 2)

# conduct a Shapiro-Wilk test on the residuals
shapiro.test(model$residuals)
```

Why will we not pay attention to this Shapiro-Wilk test result? Because the sample size is very large and Shapiro-Wilk is overly sensitive (gives false positives) at large sample sizes.

##### 3.2.2 [Conduct the test]{.underline}

```{r t-test or Wilcox}
# calculate the t-test results
t.test(CDM_TC_Sizes$shell_length_mm) # telling us if the shell lengths between sites are different enough to be statistically significant
```

#### [3.3 Graph your results using a column plot with error bars for standard error]{.underline}

For full credit, have well centered error bars and professionally labeled axes (they should not say "mean", they should say the variable name).

```{r}
CDM_TC_Sizes |>
  group_by(site) |> 
# condensing to calculate mean, standard deviation, count, and standard error
  summarise(mean_shell_length_mm = mean(shell_length_mm),
            sd_shell_length_mm = sd(shell_length_mm),
            n = n(),
            se_shell_length_mm = sd_shell_length_mm/sqrt(n)) |> 
# pipe into new ggplot
  ggplot() +
# mapping to appropriate axis
  aes(x = site, y = mean_shell_length_mm) +
# adding column bar chart where height represents group mean
  geom_col() +
# adding vertical error bars
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean_shell_length_mm - sd_shell_length_mm, 
                    ymax = mean_shell_length_mm + sd_shell_length_mm),
                         position = position_dodge(0.9),
                         width = 0.2) +
# changing default labels to appropriate labels
  labs(title = "Shell Length at CDM and Treasure Cove",
       x = "Site",
       y = "Shell Length")
```

#### [3.4 - Interpret and explain the results of your test]{.underline}

Are we pretty confident that these samples were drawn from different populations? Why is the standard error so small?

We are confident that these samples were drawn from different populations. The standard error is so small because the sample size include thousands of shell length measurements.

#### 3.6. MORE EXTRA CREDIT: conduct an ANOVA to test for differences in shell length between all four sites. Show your tests for all assumptions and make a graph.

```{r}
SizeData_2022_2025
# fitting linear model to predict shell length based on site
size_data_model <- lm(shell_length_mm ~ site, data = SizeData_2022_2025)
# creating boxplot
ggplot(SizeData_2022_2025) +
  aes(x = site, y = shell_length_mm) +

plot(size_data_model, which = 2)
# running Shapiro-Wilk test to investigate normality assumption

# running Bartlett test to check for equal variances across all sites
bartlett.test(shell_length_mm ~ site, data = SizeData_2022_2025)
```


#### 4.3 Calculate meaningful variables from our measured values

Create new columns for:

- territory area in square millimeters from the "`numbsquares`" column

- Limpet body mass from shell length (equation below is from Fenberg et al. 2013).

```{r}
All_Territories_area_mass <- All_Territories |> 
  mutate(territory_area_mm = numbsquares*19*19) |> 
  mutate(mass_g = 0.00009*size_mm ^ 3.0471)


  # create a new column for territory area in mm^2 using the "numbsquares" column
         # mesh = 19 mm x 19 mm 


  # create a new column for limpet body mass
  # formula: mass_g = 0.00009*length ^ 3.0471

```

#### 4.4. Is there a relationship between limpet size and territory size?

Explore the relationship between mass_g, and area_mm2 using scatter plots.

```{r}
# plot size_mm vs area_mm2 scatterplot with best fit regression line, no SE zone, not separated by site
All_Territories_area_mass |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = mass_g, y = territory_area_mm)) +
# adding scatter plot layer
  geom_point() +
# adding linear regression line of best fit without a standard error
```

#### 4.6. What important assumptions of tests of linear regression do these scatter plots fail? How can you tell?

```{r}

# write a linear model for the relationship, then use the plot() function on the model object to show the residuals vs. fitted values and QQ plots to assess your regression. 

## fitting linear model predicting 'mass_g' based on 'territory_area_mm' 
linear_model <- lm(mass_g ~ territory_area_mm, data = All_Territories_area_mass)
# creating and displaying four statistical plot
plot(linear_model)
```

One way to transform data that has this shape is to apply a log-transformation. Logarithmic relationships are common in biology for mass, volume, or other spatial relationships.

#### 4.7. Plot the relationship between log-transformed mass and log-transformed area. Does this relationship meet assumptions?

```{r scatterplot with regression line}
# plot a scatterplot log area on y axis by log mass_g on x axis, best fit regression line but no SE interval

All_Territories_area_mass |> ggplot() + 
  aes(x = log(mass_g), y = log(territory_area_mm)) +
# adding scatterplot layer
  geom_point() +
# adding linear regression line of best fit without a standard error
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)
```

```{r}
# write the linear model object and examine the residual and QQ plots
## fitting log-log linear model 
log_model <- lm(log(mass_g)~log(territory_area_mm), All_Territories_area_mass)
## creating residuals vs. fitted plot to check for linearity and homescedasticity
plot(log_model, which = 1)
# creating normal QQ plot to check for normality
plot(log_model, which = 2)
```

#### 4.8. What is the formula for the best fit line for the relationship between territory size and body mass in owl limpets?

```{r linear regression test summary}
# fitting log-log linear model predictng territory area on mass
All_Territories_area_mass.lm <- lm(log(territory_area_mm) ~ log(mass_g), data = All_Territories_area_mass)
# print summary
All_Territories_area_mass.lm
# print statistical summary
summary(All_Territories_area_mass.lm)
# extracting second coefficient value and save to 'slope'
slope <- coef(All_Territories_area_mass.lm)[2]
slope
```

**The formula for the best fit line can be extracted from the model summary. The two values in the Estimate column are the coefficients - (Intercept) gives the y-intercept, and the variable gives the slope.**

**log(area) = 0.8903 \* log(mass) + 8.2116**

**or**

**Y = 0.8903 + 8.2116**
